Description
A PhD studentship is available with Dr. Mitch Weegman in the Department of Biology at the University of Saskatchewan (https://www.ducks.ca/our-work/science/saskatchewan-endowed-chair/). The student will lead a research project on the population ecology of Greenland white-fronted geese, using 40-year data sets to address long-standing questions about drivers of productivity on breeding areas and subpopulation structure. 
 The Greenland white-fronted goose population has continued to decline, from a peak of 35,000 individuals in 1999 to 13,000 individuals in 2025. Productivity is the proximate mechanism for population change and there is continued uncertainty about the degree to which breeding conditions explain variation in productivity. Further, there are ~45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks (subpopulations) with hypothesized differential demographic structure contributing to the decline and winter range contraction. This PhD studentship has been developed to encourage discovery with anticipated conservation application. Our project goals are to (1) estimate the environmental drivers on breeding areas of productivity in Greenland white-fronted geese, (2) identify structure in survival and reproductive success among 45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks, and (3) connect population and individual processes linking demography with individual movement and behaviour. The student will use data from thousands of neck-collared individuals and hundreds of GPS-tagged individuals spanning 40 years. This project is an international partnership among National Parks and Wildlife Service (Ireland), Aarhus University (Denmark) and University of Saskatchewan (Canada). There will be substantial additional opportunities for the student to collaborate on other projects in population and movement ecology.
 Prerequisites: Ideal candidates will have an MSc and undergraduate degree in ecology, statistics or a closely related field, and interpersonal skills to lead discussions among collaborators. Preference will be given to those with a strong quantitative background (e.g., experience with Program R, Bayesian methods) and knowledge of migratory bird ecology and management. Students must have a valid driver’s license. The successful applicant will be expected to publish manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals and present papers at scientific meetings.
 Salary and benefits: $35,000 Canadian per year plus compensation for tuition and fees
 Start date: 1 January or 1 September 2027
 Last date to apply: 21 August 2026

 (1) Letter of interest summarizing your experience, (2) Curriculum vitae or resume, (3) University transcripts (unofficial are OK), (4) Contact information for three references.

Description
 I want to bring to your attention two open graduate student positions in the Schweikert Lab at the Department of Biology and Marine Biology at the University of North Carolina Wilmington (UNCW).  Applicants with experience in neurophysiological or behavioral approaches are preferred, though not required. 

1.        MSc in Marine Biology: Behavioral Ecology of Dynamic Color Change in Reef Fishes (starting Spring or Summer 2027) 
 2.        PhD in Integrative, Comparative, and Marine Biology: Neuroethology of Adaptive Camouflage in Flatfishes (starting Fall 2027) 

Prior to applying to the UNCW graduate program, interested students should email Dr. Lorian Schweikert (schweikertl@uncw.edu) with the following: 
·      Statement of career goals and research interests (1 page max) 
·      Resume or CV 
·      Unofficial transcripts 
·      Contact information for three references 
 Priority deadline for contacting Dr. Schweikert about the MSc position is August 16th, 2026 and for the PhD position is September 13th, 2026.Interviews for both positions will begin in early fall, though interest emails will be accepted until the positions are filled. The UNCW application deadline for the MSc position is October 15th, 2026 and for the PhD position is February 15th, 2027. 
 Program Synopsis: 
Dynamic color change allows animals such as certain marine fishes to rapidly change the color and pattern of their skin, yet knowledge is lacking about how these animals gather and process the visual information needed to make color change decisions. Recent discoveries suggest that many color-changing animals can detect light with their skin, a process known as dermal photoreception, which may work alongside the eyes to regulate color change. Our lab investigates how dermal photoreception contributes to color change in fishes and whether the skin acts as a sensory system for monitoring the environment or the animal’s own coloration. By uncovering the principles underlying distributed light sensing and adaptive camouflage, the project may inform future technologies related to bioinspired sensing and material science.

Description
The Ecohydrology lab at K-State is seeking two graduate students (MS or PhD) to start in either Spring (Jan.) 2027 or Fall (Aug.) 2027. 

About the lab: Research in the Ecohydrology Lab at K-State focuses on interactions between ecological and hydrological processes in grasslands, savannas, and shrublands. We combine approaches from plant ecophysiology, ecology, hydrology, and soil science to understand how vegetation shapes water movement and critical zone function under changing climate and land-use conditions. K-State is located in Manhattan, KS in the Flint Hills ecoregion of the Great Plains, with easy access to the Konza Prairie Biological Station. We aim to foster a fun, collaborative, supportive lab environment for students to grow their research skills and create long-lasting networks of peers, collaborators, and mentors. Research projects can be tailored to student interests, but should be relevant to at least one of the following themes: 

Research Themes: 
(1)  Subsurface impacts of land-use / land-cover change – How do woody encroachment, agriculture, and land management strategies alter the subsurface (root distributions, soil structure, etc.) in ways that influence water fluxes in grasslands? What are the consequences for local water yield? 
(2)  Plant water-use strategies and coexistence in water-limited ecosystems – How do differences in rooting and water-use strategies influence competition, coexistence, and ecosystem resilience during drought and other climate extremes? 
(3)  Drivers and consequences of preferential flow – How do root systems and rainfall characteristics (intensity, duration, etc.) interact to determine preferential flow occurrence and its ecological consequences (nutrient / pollutant / solute transport, microbial activity, carbon cycling, etc.)? 

Position details: MS and PhD positions include an annual stipend of $30,771 (paid bi-weekly) and include coverage of tuition and university fees. Students qualify for a university-subsidized health insurance plan. 

Desired Background: Applicants should hold an undergraduate degree (or higher) in ecology, biology, earth sciences, hydrology, or a related field by the time of hire. Must have strong oral / written communication skills and a willingness to work outdoors in hot weather. Previous research / field experience and coding skills (Program R) are desired but not required. 

How to Apply: Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, starting right away – please send a brief personal statement (1-pg), your CV, informal undergrad (and MS, if applicable) transcripts, and contact information for three references to Rachel Keen (rkeen@ksu.edu). 

Spring semester position – January 2027 start; applications accepted no later than September 15, 2026 
Fall semester position – August 2027 start; applications accepted no later than December 1, 2026 

Visit our lab website for more details about the application process and ongoing research projects!

Rachel Keen

Description
The Bernos F.I.S.H. lab is seeking a motivated graduate student for a funded MSc or PhD research assistantship focused on the human dimensions of fisheries in Lake Champlain, with a preferred start date of January or May 2027. In our multidisciplinary lab, we study the interactions between fish, peoples, and place. Learn more about our work on our website: https://bernoslab.wordpress.com. 

The system: Imagine Lake Champlain - a large lake nested between Vermont, New York, and Quebec with five basins differing greatly in environmental conditions and fish communities. These ecological differences support a diverse fishery targeting species such as black basses, Northern Pike, Yellow Perch, Lake Trout, Atlantic Salmon, Walleye, panfish, Bowfin, and more. Some fishers are highly specialized, targeting trophy size salmonid and bass (more than 100 bass tournaments are held on the lake annually!); others are more generalist, targeting diverse fish species close to urban centers. The largest urban centers on the lake’s shorelines are Burlington, Vermont and Plattsburg, New York: both cities are experiencing population growth and are home to an increasingly diverse community, making them a potential source of new and underrepresented participants to the fisheries. Recreational and provisional fishing, which includes both open water and ice fishing, is an important part of the local culture, recreation, and economy. Understanding how fishers interact with the fisheries of Lake Champlain  is critical for ensuring both ecological sustainability and positive recreational experiences. 

The successful candidate will develop a M.Sc. or Ph.D. thesis focused on one or more aspects of the fisheries of Lake Champlain. They may draw from human dimension research (surveys, interviews, webscrapping, etc.) and fishery techniques (e.g., sampling, telemetry, genetics). While the research questions will be refined collaboratively, the thesis is expected to contribute to our understanding of one (or more) of the following topics:

-          The “movement ecology” of fishers and fishes
-          Heterogeneity in fishing behaviours, including fishing techniques, harvest rate, motivation, preferences, and decision-making. 
-          Social and knowledge networks within fisheries systems, including patterns of connections among fishers, management agencies, community organizations, and fishery-related concepts (e.g. stocking, catch and release, commercial harvesting…).

Qualifications: We welcome applicants of all backgrounds, identities, and nationalities (i.e., international applicants are encouraged to apply). Candidates from a range of disciplines will be considered, including fisheries science, ecology, natural resources, human dimensions of natural resources, environmental studies, geography, sociology, anthropology, data science and network analysis, and other related disciplines. Students with interests in interdisciplinary research, quantitative and qualitative methods, modeling and simulations, stakeholder engagement, and social-ecological systems are especially encouraged to apply. Applicants may apply for either an MSc or PhD position. PhD applicants are typically expected to demonstrate a strong foundation for independent research, which many students develop through a master's degree, research experience, professional work, or other relevant experiences.

 How to apply: To promote a transparent and equitable selection process, we ask applicants to complete a brief Google Form (Click here) during the initial screening stage. Following this review, selected candidates will be invited for an interview. The questions are designed to help us understand your research interests and long-term career aspirations, and to determine whether this position is a match for your goals and experience. Review of applications will begin on September 1 and continue on a rolling basis until the position is filled. Applicants are encouraged to submit their materials by September 1 for full consideration. If you are encountering issues accessing the form, please contact Dr. Thais Bernos (thais.bernos@uvm.edu) directly.

The San Joaquin Valley Agricultural Sciences Center conducts research to support the sustainability, quality, and productivity of specialty crops industries across California’s Central Valley. The Commodity Protection and Quality Research Unit focuses on improving postharvest quality and reducing losses of horticultural specialty crops caused by fungal pathogens, physiological disorders, and the control of quarantine insect pests that threaten market access and export opportunities.

Research Project: This fellowship provides an immersive research and professional development experience for a postdoctoral scholar interested in postharvest fruit quality, analytical chemistry, and metabolomics. You will participate in collaborative research focused on understanding how postharvest treatments and pathogen infections influence the chemical composition, sensory characteristics, and overall quality of fresh fruits.

You will engage in analytical chemistry investigations designed to characterize volatile and non-volatile metabolites associated with fruit quality and disease responses. Research activities may include chemical profiling of fresh fruit using advanced analytical platforms such as HS-SPME-GC–MS, SIFT-MS, high-resolution mass spectrometry, and related technologies to evaluate changes in flavor compounds, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and other chemical markers. The fellowship also provides opportunities to integrate chemical data with sensory quality assessments to better understand how postharvest treatments influence aroma, flavor, and consumer-relevant quality attributes.

Throughout the fellowship, you will participate closely with a multidisciplinary research team contributing to the development and refinement of analytical workflows that support broader studies in postharvest biology, fruit metabolomics, and disease management.

Advanced analytical chemistry techniques for profiling fruit metabolites and VOCs
Operation and application of HS-SPME-GC–MS, SIFT-MS, and high-resolution mass spectrometry platforms
Experimental design and data interpretation related to postharvest fruit quality
Integration of metabolomic and sensory quality data
Research approaches for studying pathogen impacts on fresh produce
Collaborative scientific research and interdisciplinary teamwork
Development and optimization of analytical workflows and laboratory methods
Communication of scientific findings to research and industry audiences
This fellowship offers a hands-on learning environment that supports scientific skill development while contributing to research aimed at improving postharvest fruit quality, enhancing disease management strategies, and supporting agricultural and food industry resilience.

Description
M.S. Graduate Research Assistantship – Long-term Population Trends of Forest Birds in the Ozark and Ouachita National Forests

Forest birds are experiencing widespread changes in abundance and distribution due to forest succession, management, and changing environmental conditions. This research will evaluate long-term population trends and community dynamics of breeding birds in the Ozark and Ouachita National Forests by using one of the most comprehensive long-term bird monitoring datasets in the southeastern United States. The successful applicant will analyze 28 years of standardized point-count data and will conduct additional bird surveys to extend this valuable dataset.

The project will investigate how forest bird populations and communities have responded to different forest conditions across several forest types, including pine, hardwood, and mixed pine-hardwood stands. Potential research questions include: Are bird communities becoming more similar across forests or diverging over time? Are insectivores, cavity nesters, or forest interior species responding differently to forest management and forest succession? How do bird communities change as forest stands age, and do they converge toward mature forest conditions? Additional questions related to forest management and avian conservation are encouraged.

This project is expected to produce several peer-reviewed publications. Students with interests in quantitative ecology, community ecology, conservation biology, and avian ecology are especially encouraged to apply.

The successful applicant will be supported by a teaching assistantship for up to 2.5 years. Teaching duties include instructing undergraduate laboratory sections during the spring and fall semesters (typically two labs each semester). A tuition waiver is also included.

Russellville, Arkansas is a semi-rural community located in the Arkansas River Valley just south of the Ozark Mountains. Recreational opportunities include hiking, fishing, paddling, rock climbing, and mountain biking. Arkansas state parks have no entrance fees, and several are located within a short drive of campus. Arkansas Tech University has a small, close-knit graduate community where faculty are accessible and actively mentor graduate students.

Requirements: Applicants must meet the admission requirements of the Arkansas Tech University Graduate College, including a B.S. degree in wildlife biology, ecology, biology, natural resources, or a closely related field; a minimum GPA of 3.0 on a 4.0 scale; and competitive GRE scores. Applicants must also pass a background check, possess a valid driver's license with a good driving record, and be willing to work long hours under sometimes challenging field conditions. Experience identifying birds by sight and sound is highly desirable. Preference will be given to applicants with strong quantitative, analytical, and scientific writing skills. Experience with R or other statistical software is also desirable, although not required.

To be considered for this position, please email one PDF document containing: (1) a cover letter describing your interest in the position and qualifications, (2) a résumé or curriculum vitae, (3) unofficial undergraduate transcripts, and (4) If available unofficial GRE score reports showing percentiles to Dr. Chris Kellner (ckellner@atu.edu). Applications will be reviewed as they are received and will continue until the position is filled.

USGS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) located in Laurel, Maryland.

The USGS mission is to monitor, analyze, and predict current and evolving dynamics of complex human and natural Earth-system interactions and to deliver actionable intelligence at scales and timeframes relevant to decision makers. As the Nation's largest water, earth, and biological science and civilian mapping agency, USGS collects, monitors, analyzes, and provides science about natural resource conditions, issues, and problems. 

Research Project: Exposure to chemical and biological stressors can profoundly influence organismal health by reshaping gene regulation at the cellular level. This project investigates how contaminants such as PFAS and pesticides, along with environmental hazards like algal toxins, alter host transcriptomic profiles. By integrating high-resolution molecular analyses with environmental context, the study aims to identify disrupted pathways, characterize early indicators of physiological stress, and improve our understanding of mechanistic links between contaminant exposure and adverse outcomes. The research will also advance our understanding of the interplay between host and microbial genomics/transcriptomics and responses to contaminant exposure. This fellowship will facilitate interpretation of these data to train to inform science-based natural resource management by Federal, Tribal and State agencies, including the Department of War (DOW), US Fish and Wildlife Service, and US Department of Agriculture (APHIS).

Learning Objectives: This fellowship offers a unique opportunity to practice your skills in bioinformatics and develop new skills for analysis of transcriptomic and metatranscriptomic data sets collected from multiple avian species exposed to chemical (e.g. PFAS, pesticides) and/or biological/environmental (e.g. algal toxins) stressors under controlled and field conditions. Under the guidance of two mentors, you will gain experience with state-of-the-art 'omics' technologies to train to integrate field, lab, and computational datasets to address questions in wildlife toxicology and ecosystem health.

Mentor: The mentor for this opportunity is Natalie Karouna-Renier (nkarouna@usgs.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research please contact the mentor(s). 

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: August 3, 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of DOI and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: Stipend rates may vary based on numerous factors, including opportunity, location, education, and experience. If you are interviewed, you can inquire about the exact stipend rate at that time and if selected, your appointment offer will include the monthly stipend rate. The anticipated stipend is $8,535 monthly.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens and Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR) only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and USGS. Participants do not become employees of USGS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: If you have questions about the application process please email USGS@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a master's or doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields.

Description
College of the Atlantic seeks a full-time faculty member in chemistry to teach a wide range of courses to undergraduate students within our single interdisciplinary degree in human ecology. We seek a colleague who is actively interested in teaching and collaborating across disciplinary boundaries. The new faculty member will have curricular and creative control over the design of foundational and topical chemistry instruction for students at a variety of skill levels. Candidates at any career stage are welcome to apply. Candidates must have prior teaching experience and a PhD in chemistry or a related field by the anticipated start date of September 1, 2027. This is a full‑time (10-month), permanent, benefits eligible position.

The successful candidate will teach sequences in general chemistry, organic chemistry, and environmental chemistry. We are also interested in courses on: materials science, chemistry of food, green chemistry, biochemistry, geochemistry, and/or other courses that explore the intersections of chemistry with the human experience as well as the wider academic domains of the sciences, arts, and humanities. The teaching load is five courses across three 10-week trimesters (e.g., 1-2-2). Other responsibilities include mentoring and advising students, supervising senior capstone projects and independent studies, and contributing to college governance. Candidates for this position will also be expected to direct the management of chemistry teaching facilities alongside colleagues and work-study students or teaching assistants.

All COA students design individualized, interdisciplinary degrees within our Bachelor of Arts in Human Ecology. We seek a colleague who is interested in collaborating on teaching and research projects across disciplines in order to offer challenging and engaging opportunities for students with a wide range of interests. We invite imaginative thinking about how candidates might use the college’s flexible curricular structure to offer collaborative, experimental, experiential, or travel courses. COA faculty have the opportunity to develop curricular and co-curricular projects connected to the resources available on campus and in the surrounding area, including the Dorr Museum of Natural History, the college waterfront, the school’s fleet of boats, Beech Hill and Peggy Rockefeller farms, and the Cox Protectorate; the college’s field stations located on Great Duck Island, Mount Desert Rock, and in Willimantic, Maine; as well as the college’s proximity to and relationship with Acadia National Park, the Jackson Laboratory, Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory, and other local and regional communities and institutions.

Compensation
Annual salary range is $75,000 to $105,000, commensurate with experience. Benefits package includes health, dental, and life insurance, retirement, vacation, short- and long-term disability, and College of the Atlantic tuition relief for employee and dependents.

To Apply
Interested candidates should submit the following materials here, combined as a single PDF file, in the following order:
A cover letter describing their interest in and unique qualifications for this position
A curriculum vitae including contact information for three professional references
A teaching statement that describes the following: a) specific examples of their teaching experience and pedagogical approaches, b) how they engage undergraduates as student researchers both inside and outside the classroom, and c) how their experience will inform their teaching and advising at COA
Brief course descriptions (course titles and one-paragraph descriptions, not syllabi) for three potential course offerings that would complement and extend the COA curriculum

Application review will begin on November 1, with successful candidates expected to visit campus for interviews in Jan-Feb 2027. Questions about the search can be directed to the search committee chair, Dr. Sarah Hall at shall@coa.edu.
